source_document.body:
2026 SEMA Show • This Batmobile-Looking Lamborghini Temerario Is on Display at SEMA
1966 Shelby GT350 Is a Rare Survivor, Owner Turned Down $250K at Mecum, New Price Is 20 Times Less
36 photos
Photo: Mecum
Shelby Mustangs aren’t the cars to make gearheads look elsewhere. Their asking prices, on the other hand, could make even the strongest cardiac muscle lose its tempo, and temporarily disconnect brain from mouth, leading to a spontaneous eruption of vocal impressions about the situation. After all, a quarter million dollars isn’t exactly lunch money for anyone, be them at whichever end of a sale. And yet, one owner of a specific ’66 GT350 thought again of just such an offer. And denied it.
When a quarter-million-dollar offer fails to secure a 60-year-old Ford Mustang, casual observers might assume the seller had an argument with reality, and sent it to sleep on the couch for a while. On October 24, 2026, at the Mecum Dallas/Fort Worth auction in Texas, bidding on a 1966 Shelby GT350 Fastback stalled at $250,000. The vlogger from the CARFINDER YouTube channel (who is a retired used car dealer) provides a walkaround of the rare fastback which came out from under the gavel unsold.
Bearing Shelby serial number SFM6S2178, this car was the 2,178th example built for the 1966 model year, and is titled as a 1966 Ford. Its odometer displays 47,506 miles, or 76,454 kilometers, a figure that could partially justify the high reserve set by the seller. However, it’s not an unmolested survivor – it wears an older repaint in the original Ivy Green metallic livery, complemented by white racing stripes.
Under the fiberglass hood reinforced by a steel frame sits the matching-numbers K-code HiPo 289 V8, Ford’s trusty Hi-Power 4.7-liter small-block from the mid-sixties. Dressed with hollow-letter Cobra finned aluminum valve covers and an aluminum high-rise intake manifold topped by a 715-cubic-feet-per-minute Holley four-barrel carburetor, the solid-lifter powerplant delivers 306 horsepower, or 310 metric horsepower, at 6,000 rpm, and 329 lb-ft (446 Nm) of torque at 4,200 revs.
Power reaches the rear axle through a close-ratio 4-speed manual Borg-Warner T-10 gearbox. The mechanical package of SFM6S2178 also includes front disc brakes, under-ride traction bars, functional rear brake cooling scoops, and 14-inch GT6 Shelby 10-spoke alloy wheels. Inside, the black vinyl cabin retains its factory back seat delete package shelf, radio delete plate, wood-rimmed steering wheel, and dash-mounted tachometer.
As the CARFINDER host observed in Fort Worth, the aged cabin and engine bay reflect the authentic, unrestored survivor theme.
Understanding why $250,000 could not buy this Ivy Green survivor requires examining the origins of the GT350 nameplate. In 1964, Ford division chief Lee Iacocca recruited Le Mans winner Carroll Shelby to turn the new Mustang into an SCCA B-Production road racer capable of defeating Chevrolet Corvettes. When Shelby asked engineer Phil Remington how far the main office stood from the Venice fabrication shop, Remington estimated 350 feet.
Photo: Mecum That casual measurement inspired the GT350 moniker, which originally spanned six model years from 1965 to 1970 with 7,053 classic examples built before returning for 325 post-title conversions between 2011 and 2014 and 24,211 factory cars from 2015 to 2020. Launched on January 27, 1965, the inaugural 1965 model saw 562 fastbacks assembled, comprising 521 street cars, 34 GT350R race cars, a couple of R-model prototypes, four drag cars, and a street prototype .
Every 1965 Shelby GT350 was a Wimbledon White fastback powered by the 289 Hi-Po V8 through a 4-speed manual transmission. For 1966, Shelby broadened its appeal across 2,378 units (1,365 street fastbacks, 999 Hertz rental fastbacks, the GT350Hs, a pair of Hertz prototypes, four factory drag cars, one Paxton-supercharged prototype, and four special-order convertibles.
While retaining the 306-horsepower, 289-cubic-inch V8 and standard 4-speed manual gearbox, the 1966 lineup introduced a 3-speed Ford C4 automatic transmission, optional rear seats, plexiglass quarter windows, and new colors like Ivy Green. In 1967, Shelby built 1,175 restyled GT350 fastbacks—plus 26 Group II notchback racers—retaining the 289-cubic-inch V8 with 4-speed manual or 3-speed automatic transmissions.
Photo: Mecum For 1968, production shifted to Michigan, yielding 1,657 cars split between 1,253 fastbacks and 404 convertibles. Those 1968 models, including 224 Hertz fastbacks, replaced the K-code engine with a 302-cubic-inch, (4.9-liter) V8 rated at 250 horsepower (253 PS), paired with 4-speed manual or 3-speed automatic transmissions.
In 1969, Ford built 960 GT350s—821 SportsRoof fastbacks, including 151 Hertz units, and 139 convertibles—before re-vinning 318 leftover cars—261 fastbacks and 57 convertibles—as 1970 models, all using a 290-horsepower, 351-cubic-inch (5.8-liter) Windsor V8. Transmissions were unchanged: 4-speed row-your-owns or 3-speed automatic.
Decades later, Shelby American revived the badge from 2011 to 2014 on 325 post-title fastbacks and convertibles using the first-gen 5.0-liter Coyote V8 engines with 6-speed manual or automatic transmissions. Ford then produced 24,211 factory fastback coupes from 2015 to 2020 (137 in 2015, 6,169 in 2016, 7,115 in 2017, 4,378 in 2018, 3,595 in 2019, and 2,817 in 2020) equipped with a 526-horsepower 5.2-liter flat-plane-crank V8 and 6-speed manual transmission.
Photo: Mecum The current S650 Mustang brough about the fourth iteration of the fabled Shelby GT350 nameplate, again as a post-title-only machine based on the Mustang GT and its 480-hp Coyote V8 (Generation 4).
Recent auction metrics explain why the consignor of SFM6S2178 rejected $250,000 in Texas. Across 342 verified classic Shelby GT350 sales recorded over the past 5-year period by classic.com , the overall median sale price across all 1965 to 1970 model years sits at $151,200.
Over the past twelve-month period, 26 classic GT350s changed hands between $81,400 and $1,100,000, yielding a Year-To-Date median of $218,500 across all vintage years and a $310,700 average specifically for 1966 models. And that’s before factoring in the color: Ivy Green was not a commonly ordered shade on ’66 GT350s. Factory records didn’t specify the production by paint choice, but over the years, enthusiasts have compiled a database showing how scarce this specific shade is.
Photo: Mecum Of the 999 Hertz cars, just 59 came in Ivy Green; the Paxton supercharged prototype was also colored like them. The Shelby American Automobile Club estimates under 15% of production cars have been splashed Ivy Green from the factory, meaning only about 200 examples were made like the one in the gallery.
Rare, but what’s the correct price for that lack of commonality? Let me know in the comments if you have an idea. Just so you know, it’s on the market again, and the current bid is a microscopic $11k, with two more days to go. However, the Buy It Now price is $12,500, exactly 20 times under the high bid from October 24. There's also a $11,200 Facebook Marketplace listing for it (in Anchorage, Alaska), but the seller's profile would have one think the ad is a scam.
